newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Options for Creditanstalt running out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Options for Creditanstalt running out.

text.p: Austrian banking was in turmoil on Tuesday after Finance Minister Viktor Klima rejected a lone bid for flagship bank Creditanstalt and analysts said he was fast exhausting his options in the marathon sale.
The finance ministry announced late on Monday it had turned down an Austrian-Italian-German bid for Creditanstalt and was returning to the drawing board for the third time in five and a half years.

The government's sale advisor, the U.S. investment house J.P. Morgan, is to make a fresh assessment of Creditanstalt in the next six to eight weeks, laying down the timetable for a sale by the end of the year, a finance ministry source said.
"We can count on getting our money," the source said.
Analysts did not share the finance ministry's optimism, however, and noted the government's long struggle to find a buyer for Creditanstalt had become a national embarrassment.
"The situation is ridiculous...The government's options definitely have not increased after Monday's events," said Alfred Reisenberger, an analyst at IMI Sigeco in London.
"The market is bored with the whole story," said a Vienna share trader. Creditanstalt ordinary shares dipped nine schillings to 625.1 in a generally limp market.

Last year J.P. Morgan valued the government's Creditanstalt holding at 17.5 to 18.7 billion schillings ($1.65 billion to $1.76 billion). At the current share price, its stake is worth 12.6 billion schillings and the whole bank 23.5 billion.

Experts said political infighting and group interests had scuppered successive privatisation attempts and dismissed finance ministry assurances that harmony reigned in the coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party.
"There is nothing wrong with Creditanstalt. The whole thing is purely political," Reisenberger said.
The People's Party, junior partner in the coalition, has insisted on an "Austrian solution" to the privatisation of Creditanstalt, once banker to the Austro-Hungarian empire.
Successive Social Democrat finance ministers have been more concerned with filling the nation's bare coffers in an effort to pass muster for a single European currency, however.
Analysts said the infighting did not bode well for the bank's future owner.
"Any management considering buying into Creditanstalt is bound to be concerned that its hands may be tied by the government," said Robin Horne at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Thousands of job losses and hundreds of branch closures could follow if a future owner set about restructuring Creditanstalt, experts noted.
"The only people happy this morning will be the bank's employees because their jobs are more or less safe for the time being," one international analyst said.
Most market watchers agreed the Austrian-German-Italian consortium remained favourite to take over the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt's ordinary voting shares despite Monday's setback.

The group, headed by Italian insurer EA-Generali and including Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana, said it failed in its bid because it was reluctant to take on all of the government's 19.9 million shares.

Analysts said the most likely scenario was a fresh bid from the consortium, possibly including savings bank Die Erste (First Austrian). Die Erste jumped ship on September 6 after a disagreement over the form the group's bid should take.
"Either Die Erste comes back into the fray or the government can try to sell Creditanstalt to an international bank or insurer," said Kleinwort Benson's Horne.

Analysts rated the second option a long shot. Former suitors, such as Switzerland's CS Holding and Germany's Allianz, have been burned in their attempts to buy into Creditanstalt and would think twice before trying again, experts said. ($1=10.64 Schilling)
